summary: The short pronouns (mi, ti, lo, la, gli, le, si, ci, vi, li, ne) lean on a verb and cannot stand where English puts them. The idea that makes it click: ask what form the verb has. Conjugated verb: the pronoun goes in front (lo vedo, non l'ho visto). Infinitive, gerund or ecco: it is glued to the end (vederlo, vedendolo, eccolo). Modal + infinitive: either end, never the middle.

subs.label: before the conjugated verb, after non: non gli scrivo
subs.focus: In statements and questions with one conjugated verb in a simple tense, any short pronoun (direct lo / la / li / le, indirect gli / le, mi / ti / ci / vi, reflexive si, ci for a place, ne) stands directly before the verb, and non stands before the pronoun: gli scrivo, non gli scrivo, ci vado spesso, mi alzo presto, non ne voglio. Typical errors of English speakers: the pronoun after the verb (scrivo gli, vado ci, alzo mi), the pronoun before non (gli non scrivo), an adverb between pronoun and verb (lo sempre vedo). The direct pronouns are already drilled this way in direct-object-pronouns, so here use mostly indirect and reflexive pronouns, ci and ne. This is level one material and a home of order items: cut the pronoun, non and the verb as separate tiles; glue an adverb of time to another tile or list its other correct places in alts. Wrong sentences must use a form that is only a short pronoun (lo, la, li, mi, ti, gli, ci, vi, si, ne) after the verb: the stressed forms me, te, lui, lei, noi, voi are correct after a verb when there is contrast (chiamo te, non lui), so never offer them as the error. No imperatives: there the pronoun is attached (imperative topic).

subs.label: before the auxiliary: non mi ha visto, ci sono stato
subs.focus: In the passato prossimo and the other compound tenses the pronoun stands before avere or essere, and non before the pronoun: non mi ha visto, gli ho telefonato, ci sono stato, si è alzata, ne ho comprati due. It is not placed between the auxiliary and the participle and it is not attached to the participle. Typical errors: ho gli telefonato, ho telefonato gli, ha mi visto, sono ci stato, è si alzata, mi non ha visto. Order items: auxiliary and participle as separate tiles, so that the learner has to keep the pronoun out of the gap. Keep the item about position only: with lo, la, li, le and ne the participle must be written correctly agreed in every tile and option (l'ho vista, ne ho comprati due), and the choice of essere or avere must never be what is decided. Prefer mi, ti, gli, le, ci (place) and the reflexives, which raise no agreement question beyond the usual one with essere.

subs.label: glued to the infinitive, final e dropped: per vederlo, prima di alzarmi
subs.focus: When the verb the pronoun belongs to is an infinitive, the pronoun is attached to its end as one word and the infinitive loses its final e: vedere + lo = vederlo, alzare + mi = alzarmi, andare + ci = andarci, parlare + ne = parlarne; infinitives in -rre lose -re (tradurre, tradurlo). This is the only position after a preposition (per vederlo, prima di alzarmi, senza dirgli niente, invece di andarci), after è + adjective (è facile farlo), after bisogna (bisogna dirgli tutto) and after verbs such as sperare di, pensare di, decidere di (spero di vederti presto). Typical errors: the English or French order with a separate pronoun (per lo vedere, prima di mi alzare, spero di ti vedere), the pronoun written apart after the infinitive or with the e kept (vedere lo, vederelo), and the pronoun moved in front of a verb that does not allow it (lo spero di vedere, lo bisogna fare). For wrong judge sentences of this last kind use only sperare di, pensare di, decidere di and bisogna: several other verbs accept the pronoun in front (see the next two sub-points), and with fare and lasciare + infinitive the pronoun goes before fare (lo faccio riparare), so do not build items on fare or lasciare + infinitive, or on vedere and sentire + infinitive. The reflexive pronoun must match the subject (prima di alzarmi, mi lavo); write it correctly, its choice belongs to reflexive-verbs. At level three the past infinitive can be used: the pronoun attaches to avere or essere (dopo averlo letto, dopo essermi alzato); keep the participle correctly agreed. Non + infinitive as a command (non farlo) belongs to imperative.

subs.label: potere, volere, dovere, sapere: lo voglio vedere or voglio vederlo
subs.focus: With potere, volere, dovere and sapere (know how to) followed by an infinitive, the pronoun has two standard positions with the same meaning: before the modal as a separate word (lo voglio vedere, non ti posso aiutare, mi devo alzare, ci dobbiamo andare, lo sai fare?) or attached to the infinitive (voglio vederlo, non posso aiutarti, devo alzarmi, dobbiamo andarci, sai farlo?). What is wrong: the pronoun between the modal and the infinitive (voglio lo vedere, posso ti aiutare), written apart after the infinitive (voglio vedere lo), used twice (lo voglio vederlo), before non (lo non voglio vedere), or left dangling after the modal in the negative (non voglio lo vedere). Never mark one of the two standard positions wrong and never set them against each other in a cloze. In order and rewrite items the tiles decide which position is built: with separate tiles lo, voglio, vedere the only correct order has lo first; with the tile vederlo the pronoun follows the modal. Write tl to match the tiles, and do not add an extra tile that would let the learner build the other standard position; a good extra tile is a spare lo beside vederlo, which can only produce the doubled error. Rewrite items can ask to move the pronoun (Attach the pronoun to the infinitive. / Put the pronoun before the first verb.). Keep the modal in a simple tense (presente, imperfetto, futuro, condizionale): in compound tenses the auxiliary and the participle ending change with the position (mi sono dovuto alzare, ho dovuto alzarmi), which belongs to auxiliary-choice and participle-agreement. Remember that posso non farlo is correct with another meaning (I am able not to do it), so do not use it as a wrong sentence.

subs.label: cominciare a, andare a, stare per: vado a prenderlo or lo vado a prendere
subs.focus: A small group of verbs that form one unit with the infinitive behaves like the modals: cominciare a, andare a, stare per, and others such as venire a, continuare a, finire di, riuscire a. The pronoun is attached to the infinitive (comincio a capirlo, vado a prenderla, sto per chiamarti) or stands before the first verb (lo comincio a capire, la vado a prendere, ti sto per chiamare). Both are standard; the attached form is always safe and with cominciare a and stare per it is the more usual one. What is wrong: the pronoun anywhere in the middle (vado la a prendere, vado a la prendere, sto ti per chiamare, comincio lo a capire), written apart at the end (vado a prendere la) or used twice (la vado a prenderla). Build items only on cominciare a, andare a and stare per, never mark either standard position wrong, and prefer the attached form as tl in cloze items. In order items make a and per separate tiles or glue them to the first verb (vado a | prenderla), so that the learner decides where the pronoun goes. Stare + gerund is in the gerund sub-point.

subs.label: la sto leggendo or sto leggendola; alone: vedendolo
subs.focus: With stare + gerund the pronoun stands before stare (la sto leggendo, ti stavo cercando, che cosa gli stai dicendo?, mi sto preparando) or is attached to the gerund in one word (sto leggendola, stavo cercandoti). Both are standard; before stare is by far the more usual in speech, so use it as tl in most items and keep the attached form for correct judge sentences that look like a trap. What is wrong: the pronoun between stare and the gerund (sto la leggendo, sto mi preparando), written apart at the end (sto leggendo la) or used twice (la sto leggendola). A gerund without stare takes the pronoun attached, always in one word: vedendola così triste, alzandomi presto, parlandogli con calma, pensandoci bene. Typical errors there: la vedendo, mi alzando, vedendo la. The gerund alone is level two and three; stare + gerund with a pronoun can be level one in the presente. When to use stare + gerund at all belongs to gerund-and-infinitive: here the sentence is always clearly in progress.

subs.label: glued to ecco: eccolo, eccomi, eccoti il resto
subs.focus: Ecco is not a conjugated verb, so the pronoun is attached to its end in one word: eccomi, eccoci, eccolo, eccola, eccoli, eccole, and with an indirect pronoun eccoti il resto, eccovi le chiavi (here is ... for you). Typical errors: the pronoun in front or written apart (lo ecco, mi ecco, ecco lo, ecco mi), and a subject pronoun (ecco io). The choice of lo, la, li, le with ecco is already drilled in direct-object-pronouns: here keep the gender obvious and test only the position, in order items (eccola | qui | sul tavolo) and judge items. Every sentence needs at least three words, so give ecco some company (eccomi, sono pronto; dov'è la penna? eccola qui). Ecco + noun stands alone and is correct (ecco il treno): a good correct judge sentence.

subs.label: loro (to them) after the verb: ho detto loro la verità
subs.focus: Loro meaning to them is the one indirect pronoun that follows the verb, as a separate word and with no preposition: dico loro la verità, ho detto loro di aspettare, voglio parlare loro domani. It belongs to careful written Italian; in everyday speech and writing to them is gli, which goes before the verb like the other short pronouns (gli dico la verità, gli ho detto di aspettare). Both are standard, so never set gli against loro as right and wrong. Typical errors: loro placed like a short pronoun before the verb (loro dico la verità meaning to them), loro attached to an infinitive (dirloro), and gli placed after the verb like loro (dico gli la verità). In compound tenses write loro after the participle (ho detto loro); the order ho loro detto exists in bureaucratic prose, so do not use it at all, neither as right nor as wrong. A loro with the preposition is the stressed form and is free in position (a loro non ho detto niente): do not offer it as an error. Level two and three only, in sentences with a clearly formal or written tone; keep this sub-point to a small share of a batch.

rules.rule: With a conjugated verb, put the short pronoun directly in front of it. Non goes before the pronoun, and nothing comes between pronoun and verb.
rules.pattern: (non) + pronoun + verb: gli scrivo | non gli scrivo | ci vado | mi alzo | non ne voglio

examples.en: I never write to him.
I go there every summer.
I get up at seven.
I do not want any more, thank you.

rules.note: The stressed forms (me, te, lui, lei, noi, voi) are different words: they follow the verb and add contrast, as in chiamo te, non lui. Commands attach the pronoun: see the topic on the imperative.

rules.rule: In the passato prossimo the pronoun goes before avere or essere. Keep it out of the space between the auxiliary and the participle.
rules.pattern: (non) + pronoun + avere / essere + participle: non mi ha visto | ci sono stato

examples.en: Marco did not see me.
I phoned him last night.
We went there last year.
Marta got up early.

rules.rule: When the pronoun belongs to an infinitive, drop the final e of the infinitive and glue the pronoun to it: one word. After a preposition this is the only place for it.
rules.pattern: vedere + lo = vederlo | alzare + mi = alzarmi | andare + ci = andarci | per vederlo, prima di alzarmi, senza dirgli

examples.en: I have come to see you.

examples.tl: Prima di alzarmi guardo il telefono.
examples.en: Before getting up I look at my phone.
He went out without telling me anything.

examples.tl: Non è facile farlo da soli.
examples.en: It is not easy to do it on your own.

rules.note: Infinitives in -rre lose -re: tradurre, tradurlo. The stress of the verb does not move.

rules.rule: After bisogna and after verbs such as sperare di, pensare di, decidere di, the pronoun stays glued to the infinitive. It does not move in front of the first verb.
rules.pattern: spero di vederti | penso di comprarlo | ho deciso di andarci | bisogna dirgli

examples.en: I hope to see you again soon.
I am thinking of buying it tomorrow.
We have to tell him the truth.

rules.note: Only the modal verbs and a few verbs like cominciare a and andare a let the pronoun move forward: see the next rules.

rules.rule: With potere, volere, dovere and sapere + infinitive you can choose: pronoun before the modal, or glued to the infinitive. The meaning is the same.
rules.pattern: lo voglio vedere = voglio vederlo | non ti posso aiutare = non posso aiutarti

examples.en: I want to see it tonight.
I want to see it tonight.
I cannot help you today.
I cannot help you today.

rules.note: Reflexive pronouns, ci and ne do the same: mi devo alzare or devo alzarmi, ci dobbiamo andare or dobbiamo andarci, ne voglio parlare or voglio parlarne.

rules.rule: One pronoun, one place: never between the modal and the infinitive, and never at both ends.

examples.en: Tomorrow I have to get up early.
Tomorrow I have to get up early.
Can you do it by yourself?

examples.tl: Non ci possiamo andare a piedi.
examples.en: We cannot go there on foot.

rules.note: With non, the order is non + pronoun + modal (non lo so fare) or non + modal + infinitive with the pronoun (non so farlo).

rules.rule: Cominciare a, andare a and stare per work like the modals: glue the pronoun to the infinitive, or put it before the first verb. Never anywhere in the middle.
rules.pattern: vado a prenderlo = lo vado a prendere | sto per chiamarti = ti sto per chiamare

examples.en: I am going to pick him up at the station.

examples.tl: Lo vado a prendere alla stazione.
examples.en: I am going to pick him up at the station.
I am beginning to understand it now.

examples.tl: Sto per chiamarlo, aspetta un momento.
examples.en: I am about to call him, wait a moment.

rules.note: If you are not sure, glue it to the infinitive: that is always correct.

rules.rule: With stare + gerund the pronoun goes before stare, or it is glued to the gerund. Not between the two.
rules.pattern: la sto leggendo = sto leggendola | ti stavo cercando = stavo cercandoti

examples.en: I am reading it now.
I am reading it now.
I had been looking for you for an hour.
What are you telling him?

rules.note: In speech the pronoun before stare is much more common; the glued form is correct too.

rules.rule: A gerund on its own, without stare, takes the pronoun glued to its end in one word.
rules.pattern: vedendo + la = vedendola | alzando + mi = alzandomi | pensando + ci = pensandoci

examples.tl: Vedendola così triste, le ho telefonato.
examples.en: Seeing her so sad, I phoned her.

examples.tl: Alzandomi presto, ho più tempo per me.
examples.en: By getting up early, I have more time for myself.
Thinking about it carefully, you are right.

rules.rule: After ecco, glue the pronoun to the end and write one word.
rules.pattern: eccomi | eccoci | eccolo | eccola | eccoli | eccole | eccoti il resto

examples.en: Here I am, I am ready!
Where is the pen? Here it is.
Here is your change.

rules.note: With a noun, ecco stands alone: ecco il treno.

rules.rule: Loro meaning to them goes after the verb, as a separate word and with no preposition. It is formal; in everyday Italian say gli, which goes before the verb.
rules.pattern: dico loro la verità (formal) | gli dico la verità (everyday)

examples.en: I told them the truth.

examples.tl: Il professore spiega loro la regola.
examples.en: The teacher explains the rule to them.
I told them the truth.

rules.note: Gli ho detto can also mean I told him: the context decides. Loro is never glued to a verb: dire loro, two words.

right.en: I write to him every week.

contrasts.why: Scrivo is a conjugated verb, so the short pronoun cannot follow it as him does in English. It goes in front: gli scrivo.
Nothing separates the pronoun from its verb. Non stands before the pronoun: non mi ha visto.
In the passato prossimo the pronoun goes before the auxiliary, not between ho and the participle: gli ho telefonato.

right.en: I have come to see you.

contrasts.why: After a preposition the verb is an infinitive, and the pronoun is glued to its end with the final e dropped: vedere + ti = vederti.

right.en: I want to see it tonight.

contrasts.why: The pronoun cannot stand between the modal and the infinitive. Glue it to the infinitive (voglio vederlo) or put it before the modal (lo voglio vedere).

right.en: I want to see it tonight.

contrasts.why: The two positions are a choice, not a pair: the pronoun is said once. Either lo voglio vedere or voglio vederlo.

right.en: I hope to see you again soon.

contrasts.why: The pronoun never stands as a separate word before an infinitive. It is attached to the end: rivedere + ti = rivederti.
With stare + gerund the pronoun goes before stare (la sto leggendo) or is glued to the gerund (sto leggendola), not between the two.

contrasts.wrong: La vedendo così triste, le ho telefonato.

right.tl: Vedendola così triste, le ho telefonato.
right.en: Seeing her so sad, I phoned her.

contrasts.why: A gerund without stare is not a conjugated verb, so the pronoun does not go in front. It is glued to the end: vedendola.

right.en: I want to tell them the truth.

contrasts.why: Loro is not glued to the verb like gli or lo. It follows as a separate word: dire loro. The everyday form is voglio dirgli la verità.

cheat: Conjugated verb: pronoun in front, non before the pronoun. Non gli scrivo.
Passato prossimo: before avere or essere. Non mi ha visto, ci sono stato.
Infinitive: drop the e and glue it on. Per vederlo, prima di alzarmi, spero di vederti.
Potere, volere, dovere, sapere: lo voglio vedere or voglio vederlo. Never in the middle, never twice.
Cominciare a, andare a, stare per: the same choice. Glued to the infinitive is always safe.
Sto + gerund: la sto leggendo (or sto leggendola). Gerund alone and ecco: glued, vedendolo, eccolo.
Loro (to them, formal) follows the verb as its own word: dico loro. Everyday: gli dico.
